question_text: Find the I.F. of the differential equation (cosx)dy/dx + y·sinx = tanx by transforming it into linear form.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite in linear form and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide throughout by cosx to make the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1.
steps.memory_tip: sinx/cosx = tanx is the simplification that turns the coefficient of y into the plain tanx used as P.
lines: This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
steps.why: Dividing every term by cosx makes the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1, which is what the standard linear form requires, and simplifies sinx/cosx to the plain tanx that becomes P.
common_mistakes: Dividing only the y term by cosx and forgetting to divide tanx on the right side as well.
Leaving P as sinx/cosx instead of simplifying it to the standard tanx.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: The last mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx); ∫tanx dx = log(secx) is a standard integral.
steps.memory_tip: ∫tanx dx = log|secx| — always simplifies the I.F. down to a plain trig function once exponentiated.
lines: Here P = tanx ⇒ ∫P dx = ∫tanx dx = log(secx)
steps.why: The standard integral of tanx is log(secx), and e raised to a log cancels back to the plain expression inside it, so the integrating factor simplifies all the way down to secx.
common_mistakes: Integrating tanx as −log(cosx) and then not simplifying e^(−log(cosx)) correctly to secx.
Stopping at I.F. = e^(log secx) without simplifying it down to the plain secx.
